newsitem.title: UK: Major faces crunch summit, possibly his last.
newsitem.headline: Major faces crunch summit, possibly his last.

text.p: John Major flies to Dublin on Thursday for what could be his last European summit as British prime minister, but he is unlikely to get a warm welcome from his fellow European leaders.

The best Major can hope for as the summit starts on the ill-starred Friday 13th is that his actions in the Irish capital will not trigger another bout of squabbling over Europe in his battered and divided Conservative party.
Polls now give Major little chance of winning an election due within five months and ensuring a fifth consecutive Conservative term of office.
An opinion poll in the newspaper The Times on Thursday gave the Conservatives 30 percent support, down three points on a month ago. Labour was up one point to 51 percent.

The loss of Major's overall parliamentary majority is set to be confirmed on Thursday night when the opposition is almost certain to win a by-election in the staunchly Labour seat of Barnsley East, a former coal mining area.
But even that 323-323 seat House of Commons stalemate belies the true scale of the prime minister's woes.

Although Major can rely on nine Unionist politicians from Northern Ireland to extend his term to the last gasp, one of his fractious rank and file members of parliament -- worried at his electoral prospects -- has quit the parliamentary party.

Other Conservative members, appreciating the increased leverage Major's rapidly dwindling majority gives them over the government, are now threatening the same withdrawal of support if Major does not follow their line on Europe.
With these threats coming from both pro-Europeans and "Eurosceptics" opposed to further moves to European integration, Major is once again caught between a rock and a hard place.

His fellow European leaders, angered at Major's constant attacks on Europe and his delaying tactics designed to ease domestic pressure on him from the Eurosceptics, are increasingly seeing him as a lame duck leader whose time may soon be up.

Many cannot forgive him for Britain's campaign of non-cooperation following the mad cow disease crisis which overshadowed the EU summit in June in Florence. Britain stopped its campaign when the EU gave it hope a beef export ban would be lifted.

Major this week acknowledged there was no love lost between him and many of his European colleagues, although he told the House of Commons it was because they believed Labour leader Tony Blair would be "a very easy ride".

European Commission President Jacques Santer underlined growing frustration with London on Wednesday, saying in a clear shot at Major that countries had to accept reforms if they wanted to make Europe work after it admitted new members.
But Major, urged on by his pro-European finance minister Kenneth Clarke, will tread his habitual tightrope in Dublin.

He will once again try to influence debate on moves towards reforms of the bloc and a European single currency, while at the same time saying he may well not join the currency and will block reforms unless a deal is done on a row over working hours.
Tabloid newspapers are already speculating that Major may stage some spat at the summit to please his Eurosceptics and reinforce his position ahead of the election.
But European leaders, by now resigned to leaving a deal on the reforms until the next summit in mid-1997 in Amsterdam, well after Britain's election, are unlikely to pay much attention.
